row.note: The commentary calls 1:2 a verb-less verdict whose praise is already located before a human says it; this psalm says silence itself is praise before God in Zion, making unspoken praise intelligible.

The commentary treats sun, moon, and stars as created signs rather than the Lord; this summons those same heavenly bodies to praise their Maker, giving the celestial lights a liturgical role without deifying them.
The commentary says every created kind bears witness to its Lord; here the sea and its creatures, including the depths, are directly summoned into praise.
The commentary extends the Lord's care to herds and every kind of creature; this verse includes wild and domestic animals among the voices summoned to praise.
The commentary says the plural worlds include all created kinds; this verse brings rulers, nations, and peoples into the same cosmic summons to praise.
The commentary reads each kind as a sign by which its Lord is known; the heavens here declare God's glory without a human speaker, making creation itself a witness.
The commentary says all things praise in a language humans do not understand; this verse says the heavens' testimony has no ordinary speech or words, closely matching praise beyond human hearing.
The commentary makes the created signs universal; the heavens' line and words reach the end of the world, so their testimony is not confined to one worshiping community.
The commentary says nonhuman creation praises God before a human voice is heard; Job pictures the morning stars singing together as earth's foundations are laid.
The commentary names the Lord of all worlds; Nehemiah addresses the one who made heaven, earth, sea, and all in them, keeps them alive, and receives worship from heaven's host.
The commentary includes every kind in the Lord's domain; Isaiah says wilderness animals honor God because he supplies water in the desert.
The commentary says praise belongs to God independently of a human speaker; Isaiah says the people God formed are meant to recount his praise.

The commentary says every thing praises God in its own way; Revelation gives a cosmic liturgy in which every creature in heaven, earth, under earth, and sea voices blessing and honor to the One on the throne and the Lamb.
The commentary assigns praise to God as Lord of all worlds; the elders here give glory and honor to the one worthy because he created all things and they exist by his will.
The commentary distinguishes the sun and moon as signs from the Lord they indicate; the angel calls people to worship the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs of water.
The commentary expands the ordinary title Rabb into Lord of all worlds; Paul calls the maker of the world and everything in it Lord of heaven and earth.
The commentary says praise does not originate in human speech; Paul says God is not served as though he needed anything, since he himself gives life and breath to all.
The commentary identifies God as Lord of all worlds; Paul tells the crowd to turn from vain things to the living God who made heaven, earth, sea, and all that is in them.
The commentary develops the Rab image through cloud, water, pasture, and herd; Paul names rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness as gifts from the Creator.
The commentary reads heavenly bodies as signs within the created world, not as its Lord; Genesis assigns the lights the task of marking seasons, days, and years.
The commentary's Abraham scene rejects stars, moon, and sun as rulers over their Maker; Genesis places the two great lights among the things God made and appointed to govern day and night.
The commentary calls each created kind a sign by which the Lord is known; Wisdom says people who infer no knowledge of God from visible good things fail to recognize their maker through his works.
The commentary says the worlds are signs that show their Lord; Wisdom argues that the beauty of created things should lead their observer to perceive the maker.
The commentary treats the whole creation as a field of divine signs; Wisdom says the greatness and beauty of creatures give a proportionate way to perceive their creator.
The commentary says creatures are signs by which their Lord is recognized; Paul says God's unseen power and divinity are perceived through what has been made.
The commentary presents praise as the proper verdict on God; Paul describes people who knew God yet failed to glorify or thank him, showing the opposite response to creation's testimony.
The commentary's Abraham rejects a created light as Lord because it sets; Paul condemns exchanging the Creator's glory for worship of created things, including heavenly and earthly forms.
The commentary's Abraham refuses the setting sun and moon as possible lords; Job's speaker swears that seeing the bright sun or splendid moon did not turn him toward their worship.
The commentary makes the refusal of celestial worship the test of who remains Lord; Job names the hidden temptation of the heart and the hand's kiss to the moon as forbidden worship.
The commentary says the bodies that set are signs, not the enduring Lord; Job says such worship would deny God above and be a culpable offense.

row.basis: do not worship the host of heaven
row.note: The commentary identifies the sun, moon, and stars as created signs that cannot be Rabb; Moses warns Israel not to be drawn into worshiping those lights, which the Lord allotted to peoples under heaven.

The Qur'anic Abraham tests the star and rejects it when it sets; Genesis instead has God show Abram the stars as a measure of promised descendants, making the same sky a sign of God's word rather than an object of worship.
The commentary's Abraham turns from transient lights to their creator; in Genesis Abram responds to God's promise through the stars by trusting the speaker, not treating the stars as his lord.
The commentary says hamd is the verdict that belongs to the doer of the praised work; Melchizedek blesses God Most High as maker of heaven and earth and as the one who delivered Abram's enemies.
The commentary rejects drawing praise to oneself for a good whose source lies elsewhere; Abram refuses the king of Sodom's goods so he cannot claim to have made Abram rich.
The commentary says hamd exceeds thanks for relief but still includes response to received good; Moses commands Israel to bless the Lord after eating and being satisfied.
The commentary exposes the person who locates the source of a gift in himself; Moses warns against saying one's own power and strength acquired the wealth.
The commentary returns praise to the source of every good work; Moses says the Lord gives the power to produce wealth and thereby keeps the covenant.

row.basis: heaven and earth belong to God
row.note: The commentary names Allah as the one to whom all praise belongs and Rabb of all worlds; David's prayer says greatness, power, glory, victory, and majesty are God's because all in heaven and earth is his.
The commentary attaches praise to the one who did the work; David and the gathered people thank and praise God's glorious name after naming his universal kingdom.
The commentary opposes human appropriation of credit for what was given; David asks what the people can give when everything comes from God and what they offer is already his.
The commentary calls God the Rabb of all worlds; this psalm grounds the claim in God's ownership of the earth, its fullness, and its inhabitants.

The commentary's Rab imagery includes owner, herd, pasture, and the one who tends; the psalm says God made the people and calls them his flock, then brings them to worship with thanksgiving and praise.
The commentary stretches the limited human use of Rabb to the Lord of all worlds; this verse says God's throne is established in heaven and his kingdom rules over all.
The commentary says the praise of creation is not produced by the human reader; the psalm summons all God's works, everywhere in his dominion, to bless him.
The commentary says every created kind knows its Lord through signs; this verse says all God's works give thanks while his faithful ones bless him.
The commentary identifies the Rabb of all worlds; the next line has worshipers speak of the glory and power of God's kingdom to make it known.
The commentary's Rab field includes nurture, water, pasture, and herds; the psalm says God opens his hand and satisfies the desire of every living thing.
The commentary links Rabb with the cloud that grows plants and sustains herds; this psalm says all creatures wait for God to give them food in its season.
The commentary develops the layered cloud that waters plants and pasture; this verse says God covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow on the mountains.
The commentary moves from cloud and water to the herd that remains where it is fed; this verse says God gives animals their food and feeds the young ravens.
The commentary joins the cloud that grows plants with hamd as a judgment that a place is good to inhabit; the psalm describes God watering furrows and softening the soil for grain.
The commentary brings Rab, abundant water, pasture, and a herd that stays together into one scene; this verse clothes the pastures with flocks and has valleys shout and sing.

The commentary's Rab branches include an owner and a herd, while its prose describes nurture as bringing a being toward completion; the psalm pictures the Lord as shepherd who gives pasture and still water.
The commentary joins the owner of the herd with the lost animal and the nurturing Rabb; Ezekiel says God himself seeks the lost, brings back the strayed, binds the injured, and strengthens the weak.

The commentary couples praise with Rabb of all worlds; Jesus blesses the Father as Lord of heaven and earth, and the context says revelation is given to little ones rather than self-assured wise people.

row.basis: all things from and to God
row.note: The commentary returns every praiseworthy deed to its source and calls God Rabb of all worlds; Paul says all things are from, through, and toward God, to whom glory belongs forever.

The commentary develops the image of the Rabb as the one who keeps a diverse plurality from scattering; Colossians says all things cohere in Christ, offering a Christian formulation of that sustaining relation.
The commentary contrasts praise returned to its source with a person claiming a gift as his own; Paul asks what anyone has that was not received, and therefore why boast as if it were not received.
The commentary warns against pulling praise toward oneself; Jeremiah forbids boasting in wisdom, strength, or wealth and directs boasting toward understanding and knowing the Lord.
The commentary criticizes the person who draws praise to himself for his own acts; Proverbs says praise should come from another's mouth, not one's own.
The commentary opposes claiming credit and praise for oneself; Jesus warns against practicing righteousness in order to be seen by people, shifting recognition to the Father who sees in secret.

The commentary's false claimant wants praise for himself; in Jesus' parable the Pharisee's prayer thanks God but immediately boasts of his own virtue, while the following tax collector asks for mercy.

row.basis: tax collector rather than self-exalting Pharisee
row.note: The commentary separates genuine praise from self-congratulation; Jesus says the humbled tax collector goes home justified, while the one exalting himself is brought low.
The commentary notes hamd after the unjust people's destruction as a verdict, not gratitude for a gift; Revelation's multitude gives glory and power to God after the judgment of Babylon.

row.basis: God's judgments are true and just
row.note: The commentary says hamd can approve the right outcome after a judgment; Revelation explicitly praises God because his judgments are true and just and he has judged the corrupting power.
The commentary's exact hamd formula follows the cutting off of a wicked people; Moses' song begins after Egypt's army is defeated and praises the Lord for triumph over the oppressor.
The commentary joins creation's praise with the final judgment that sets things right; this psalm has the sea roar before the Lord who comes to judge the world.
The commentary says nonhuman creation praises in ways people do not grasp; the rivers clap and hills sing before the Lord in the same scene that announces his righteous judgment.

row.basis: the Lord judges all the earth
row.note: The commentary's hamd after judgment is a verdict on what is right; this verse says the Lord comes to judge the earth with righteousness and the peoples with equity.
The commentary says creation's praise is not a human performance; David's public worship song has the trees sing before the Lord because he comes to judge the earth.

The commentary says hamd is a judgment broader than thanking someone for an advantage; the Mishnah requires a person to bless God for misfortune as for good fortune, making praise independent of immediate relief.

The commentary says praise belongs to the source of every good rather than to the person who receives it; the Talmud treats enjoyment of the world without a blessing as misappropriating what belongs to God.
The commentary says each created kind is a sign of its Lord and that praise is not dependent on a human speaker; this rabbinic saying gives the purpose of all creation as the Creator's glory.

row.ref: Adon Olam, opening and closing stanzas
row.note: The commentary calls God Lord of all worlds and says the Lord remains when transient things pass; the hymn praises the Lord who precedes creation and reigns alone after all things cease.
The commentary says the worlds are signs through which the Lord is known; Augustine questions earth, sea, sky, sun, moon, and stars, and each directs him beyond itself to its maker.

row.ref: Song of the Three Youths, Greek Daniel 3:57–88
row.basis: all works summoned to bless God
row.note: The commentary says every thing praises God in its own manner; this hymn lists works of creation and summons them to bless and exalt the Lord. Numbering differs across editions.

row.basis: Hebrew rab as teacher or master
row.note: The commentary's Arabic dictionary glosses Rabb as owner, obeyed master, and one who sets things right; the Mishnah's Hebrew cognate rab is a human teacher one appoints, preserving the master-teacher sense without claiming it means Lord of all worlds.
The commentary glosses Rabb as owner and obeyed master; Daniel's Aramaic uses rab for a human chief set over other officials, a concrete cognate in a limited social relation.
The commentary includes master and nurturing teacher among the senses heard alongside Arabic Rabb; John's disciples address Jesus with the Semitic title Rabbi and the narrator explains it as Teacher.

The commentary labels Arabic hamd from h-m-d as praise and a verdict of worth; the Hebrew cognate in this verse describes the Lord's instruction as desirable, a related evaluative sense rather than a word for praise.

The commentary says praise precedes the human reciter and belongs to the Lord; the Psalter closes by summoning everything with breath to praise the Lord, placing the ayah's opening verdict beside a book's final doxology.

row.basis: all creation praises the exalted name
row.note: The commentary says every created kind is a sign of its Lord; the psalm's conclusion gathers heaven and earth under praise because the Lord's name alone is exalted.
The commentary makes created kinds signs by which their Lord is known; Job tells the hearer to ask beasts and birds, which can teach this truth.
The commentary extends signs beyond human speech; Job says to speak to the earth and sea creatures, which can teach the inquirer.
The commentary says the worlds point beyond themselves to their Lord; Job asks who does not know from these creatures that the Lord's hand made them.

row.basis: life and breath in God's hand
row.note: The commentary calls God Rabb of all worlds; Job says the life of every living thing and the breath of all humanity are in God's hand.
The commentary presents the worlds as signs of their Lord and names praise as the right judgment; this psalm asks that the Lord's glory endure and says he rejoices in his works.
The commentary reads hamd after a wicked people's destruction as a verdict on the right outcome; Psalm 104 ends by asking that sinners vanish and then turns to blessing the Lord.

row.basis: name praised from sunrise to sunset
row.note: The commentary discusses the sun as a created light that can be mistaken for a deity; this psalm uses sunrise and sunset to frame praise of the Lord's name everywhere.
The commentary calls God owner of every world and develops the herd as an image; this psalm says every forest animal and cattle on the hills already belong to God.
The commentary says praise is God's due even when human speech or gratitude supplies nothing; the psalm says God would not need to tell humans if hungry, because the world and its fullness are his.
The commentary pairs the Lord of worlds with the knowledge by which created signs are recognized; Proverbs says the Lord founded earth by wisdom and established the heavens by understanding.
The commentary's prose brings the knowing sign-world together with the rain cloud that grows plants; Proverbs links God's knowledge to the bursting deeps and the clouds that drip dew.

row.basis: gods that did not create will perish
row.note: The commentary's Abraham rejects setting luminaries as lords and turns to the Creator; Jeremiah's Aramaic sentence says gods that did not make heaven and earth will perish from earth and under heaven.

The commentary calls God Rabb of all worlds and contrasts the abiding Lord with transient lights; Jeremiah says God made earth by power, established the world, and stretched out the heavens by understanding.

row.basis: God carries Israel as a son
row.note: The commentary hears in Rabb the raising of a child through successive stages; Moses recalls God carrying Israel through the wilderness as a man carries his son.

row.basis: God teaches a child to walk
row.note: The commentary's nurturing sense of Rabb is a gradual bringing to maturity; Hosea pictures God teaching Ephraim to walk and taking him by the arms.
The commentary links Rabb to nurture and the provision that brings life to completion; Hosea describes God drawing Israel with bonds of love and bending down to feed them.
The commentary develops Rabb as the one who sustains a being from its earliest state; Isaiah says God has carried the house of Jacob from birth and from the womb.
The commentary says the Rabb brings a creature through its stages to completion; Isaiah promises to carry and rescue the people even into old age and gray hairs.
The commentary says the Lord's care extends to all created kinds; Wisdom says God loves everything that exists and would not have made anything he hated.
The commentary calls God Rabb of all worlds; Wisdom says God spares all things because they are his and names him lover of life.

row.basis: bless the maker at natural signs
row.note: The commentary develops sun, moon, stars, mountains, water, and marks as created signs; this Mishnah prescribes blessings on seeing mountains, seas, the sun, moon, and stars, directing recognition to the Maker of creation.
The commentary distinguishes the heavenly lights from the Lord they indicate; Sirach describes the stars as the beauty of heaven and an ordered display in God's heights.
The commentary says hamd can be the final word after a work reaches its limit, yet Fatiha places it at the beginning; Sirach says many words still fall short and makes God the final word.
The commentary says every world is a sign but cannot be the Lord; Sirach asks where strength can be found to praise God, who is greater than all his works.
The commentary says hamd names the full, final praise due to God; Sirach commands praise as much as possible and immediately says God surpasses it.
The commentary says each thing praises in its own language even when humans do not understand; this Jewish hymn assigns scriptural praise lines to heaven, earth, and sea as their own utterances.

The commentary distinguishes sun and rain as gifts within God's world and describes Rabb as nurturer; Jesus says the Father makes the sun rise and sends rain on both evil and good, showing provision beyond human merit.
The commentary's Rabb imagery includes the owner and sustainer of a herd; Jesus points to birds that neither sow nor gather yet are fed by the heavenly Father.

row.basis: stones cry if people are silent
row.note: The commentary says praise is already located before a human reciter and does not depend on the reader's voice; Jesus says that if his disciples were silent, the stones would cry out.

The commentary contrasts the Lord who remains with celestial bodies that set and says every good belongs at its source; James calls every good gift from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow from turning.

row.basis: Lord who founded earth and heavens
row.note: The commentary calls the abiding one Rabb of all worlds; Hebrews addresses the Son as Lord and says he founded the earth and heavens, a Christian application of creator-Lord language.

The commentary's Abraham rejects lights that set and its later passage says all on earth perishes while the Lord remains; Hebrews says the created heavens and earth wear out while the addressed Lord remains.
The commentary's contrast is between passing worlds and the abiding Lord; Hebrews says creation will be changed like a garment while the Lord stays the same and his years do not fail.

row.basis: earth and fullness belong to the Lord
row.note: The commentary says all praise and every good belong to the creator rather than a human possessor; Paul quotes the psalmic claim that the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord while discussing food from the market.

The ayah assigns all hamd to Allah; Revelation's universal doxology addresses blessing, honor, glory, and might to both the one on the throne and the Lamb, preserving a distinct Christian account of who receives cosmic praise.

row.basis: only Sovereign and King of kings
row.note: The commentary says Rabb without qualification belongs to the enduring Lord of all worlds; Paul calls God the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords.
The commentary contrasts the setting lights with the Lord who remains; Paul says God alone has immortality and ascribes eternal honor and power to him.
